content: Motherwort, scientifically known as Leonurus cardiaca, is a flowering plant that belongs to the mint family, Lamiaceae. It is also commonly referred to as Throw-wort, Lion's Ear, and Lion's Tail, though the latter two names are also used for Leonotis leonurus. Originally native to Central Asia, this plant has spread globally, primarily due to its use as an herbal remedy. Leonurus cardiaca is characterized by its square stems and opposite leaves. The basal leaves are wedge-shaped with three distinct points, while the upper leaves are more intricately lobed. The plant produces flowers in the leaf axils on its upper sections, typically blooming from June to August. These flowers are small, ranging in color from pink to lilac, and often feature a furry lower lip. Motherwort grows to a height of approximately 60 to 100 cm and is commonly found along roadsides, in vacant fields, and in other disturbed or waste areas. Medicinal Uses Motherwort has a long history of medicinal application, with its use originating in Central Europe and Asia, though it has also been widely utilized in North America. The plant is highly regarded for its nourishing properties, comparable to those of stinging nettle or dandelion. It contains the alkaloid leonurine, which acts as a mild vasodilator and exerts a relaxing effect on smooth muscles. Due to these properties, motherwort has traditionally been used as a cardiac tonic, nervine, and emmenagogue. In addition to leonurine, the plant contains a variety of bioactive compounds, including bitter iridoid glycosides, diterpenoids, flavonoids (such as rutin and quercetin), tannins, volatile oils, and vitamin A. These constituents contribute to its therapeutic effects. Midwives have historically employed motherwort for various purposes, including as a uterine tonic and to prevent uterine infections. Herbalist Susun Weed recommends its use for alleviating stress and promoting relaxation during pregnancy, and she claims that it can prevent hemorrhage when administered during labor. However, Michael Tierra advises against its internal use during pregnancy, as it may cause bleeding and potentially induce miscarriage. Historically, in China, motherwort was used to prevent pregnancy and regulate menstruation. Motherwort is also utilized to relieve stomach gas, cramping, menopausal symptoms, and insomnia. However, Susun Weed cautions that regular use of motherwort for combating sleeplessness may lead to dependency. According to Michael Tierra, in traditional Chinese medicine, motherwort is described as having a bitter, spicy, and slightly cold energy, with its effects targeting the pericardium and liver systems. The plant's fresh or dried leaves are used medicinally. The standard preparation involves infusing one ounce of the herb in one pint of boiling water. Alternatively, a tincture can be used, with a recommended dosage of 10 to 30 drops taken three times daily.
